question_prompt: What are the aim and objectives of the 10-week conservation project?
text: Overall Aim: To conserve, maintain, and monitor 10 Flacourtia montana seedlings at Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park over a period of 10 weeks through systematic field-based conservation practices. Specific Objectives: (1) Identify and document the initial condition of the 10 seedlings (locations, height, health, site conditions); (2) Protect seedlings from avoidable physical damage, trampling, and grazing; (3) Provide maintenance including supplemental watering, organic mulching (keeping a gap around the stem), and non-destructive weed management; (4) Regularly monitor survival, health, pests, disease, and growth; (5) Maintain field observations and photographic documentation; (6) Develop practical conservation skills among the 6 students; (7) Prepare a baseline record and recommendations for continued park maintenance after the 10-week period.

question_prompt: What is the week-by-week schedule for the 10-week conservation project?
text: 10-Week Work Plan: Week 1: Baseline survey; identification/tagging of 10 seedlings; initial photographs; record height, health, and site conditions. Week 2: Site cleaning, removal of competing weeds where necessary, and installation/repair of protective measures. Week 3: Watering as required; mulching; first detailed health observation. Week 4: Growth and survival monitoring; weed management; photographic documentation. Week 5: Water management; inspection for pests, disease, and physical damage; corrective maintenance. Week 6: Mid-term assessment of all 10 seedlings; update growth and health records. Week 7: Continued maintenance, watering where required, protection, and weed management. Week 8: Growth monitoring and photographic documentation; assess effectiveness of conservation measures. Week 9: Final maintenance cycle; identify seedlings requiring additional attention; compile field records. Week 10: Final assessment; compare baseline and final observations; prepare project report and recommendations for continued care.

question_prompt: How are responsibilities divided among the six students?
text: Team Structure (rotatable roles): Student 1: Project coordination and activity scheduling. Student 2: Seedling health and survival monitoring. Student 3: Watering and maintenance coordination. Student 4: Weed management and site maintenance. Student 5: Measurement, data recording, and documentation. Student 6: Photography, reporting, and record compilation.

question_prompt: What indicators are monitored for each seedling and what are the project deliverables?
text: Monitoring Indicators: Number of seedlings surviving out of 10; seedling height at baseline and final assessment; visible signs of new growth; general plant health; pest/disease incidence; physical damage; soil moisture/site condition; effectiveness of protective measures; and maintenance activities completed. Deliverables: Baseline inventory of the 10 seedlings, weekly activity/maintenance records, seedling monitoring sheets, photographic documentation, mid-term observation report, final 10-week conservation report, and recommendations for continued maintenance.

question_prompt: What is out of scope or restricted in this project?
text: Project Boundaries: Limited strictly to the conservation and monitoring of the 10 identified Flacourtia montana seedlings within Dr. Sree Sree Sivakumara Swamiji Biodiversity Park. Does NOT include large-scale plantation, removal of established vegetation, chemical treatment, construction work, or changes to the park's existing management practices unless specifically authorized by park authorities.

question_prompt: What is the scientific classification and what are the local/common names of Flacourtia montana?
text: Accepted Scientific Name: Flacourtia montana J. Graham (published 1839, Cat. Pl. Bombay). Taxonomy: Kingdom Plantae | Clade Tracheophytes, Angiosperms, Eudicots, Rosids | Order Malpighiales | Family Salicaceae (formerly Flacourtiaceae) | Genus Flacourtia | Species F. montana. Common English Name: Mountain Sweet Thorn. Regional & Local Names: Kannada: Gajale, Hennu sampige, Nayibela, Champe Hannu; Marathi/Western Ghats: Atkin, Raan Tambut, Attak; Tulu: Tabluka; Malayalam: Charal-maram, Vayyamkatha.

question_prompt: How tall does Flacourtia montana grow and what does its trunk look like?
text: Flacourtia montana is a native Indian tree (often deciduous or semi-evergreen) that can attain a height of 8 m to 25 m and a trunk girth up to 1.7 m. The trunk and branches are armed with sharp, stout woody thorns (especially at the base, up to ~5 cm long). Bark is brownish to grey, thin, and smooth with a cream blaze. Young branches and twigs are hirsute/pubescent (covered with soft, dense hairs), and young leaves are reddish.

question_prompt: How do you identify the leaves, flowers, and fruits of Flacourtia montana?
text: Leaves: Simple, alternate phyllotaxy; pubescent petiole 0.3-0.9 cm long; lamina 7-15 cm (up to 18 cm) x 4-8 cm, elliptic-oblong with an acuminate (tapering) apex, crenate or crenate-serrate (toothed) margin, and 3-5 prominent nerves at the base with 4-7 pairs of secondary nerves. Leaves often turn brown on drying (unlike F. indica). Flowers: Small (~4 mm across), greenish-yellow, unisexual (dioecious—male and female flowers on separate trees), borne in compact axillary cymes or panicles; petals absent, sepals 4-5. Flowering and fruiting typically occur April-June. Fruits: Spherical/ovoid-globose fleshy berries, 1-1.8 cm across, smooth or distinctly ribbed, scarlet red to reddish-purple when ripe, containing 5-6 compressed, rough, woody seeds in 2 rows.

question_prompt: Where does Flacourtia montana grow naturally?
text: Flacourtia montana is native to southern Asia and endemic to the semi-evergreen, evergreen, and moist deciduous forests of the Western Ghats of India (up to 1000-1800 m elevation) across Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and Kerala. It thrives in humid tropical conditions, often forming part of the forest understory, secondary vegetation, or sacred groves, and supports frugivorous birds and wildlife through its fruit production.

question_prompt: What are the culinary, nutritional, and medicinal uses of Flacourtia montana?
text: Culinary & Nutrition: Ripe scarlet-red fruits are edible raw (sweet and slightly astringent, similar to gooseberry) and can be processed into juices, jams, jellies, preserves, pickles (tender fruits), and wine. Fruits are rich in ascorbic acid (vitamin C), carotenoids, anthocyanins, flavonoids, phenolic compounds, calcium, and iron. Traditional Medicine (Ayurveda & Ethnobotany): Infusions of bark, leaves, and roots are used for fever, diarrhoea, inflammation, diabetes, microbial infections, and as a gargle for hoarseness. Leaves are used as a carminative, astringent, tonic, expectorant, and anthelmintic. Other Uses: Bark is used for tanning; wood is used for agricultural implements such as ploughs.

question_prompt: How is Flacourtia montana propagated and what are its nursery challenges?
text: Seed Propagation: Seed-based propagation faces challenges due to intermediate seed storage behavior and declining seed viability over time, though appropriate pre-treatments and controlled storage improve germination rates. Vegetative Propagation: Studies (Rasmi & Jose, 2025) show that vegetative propagation using stem cuttings and layering treated with growth regulators such as indole-3-butyric acid (IBA) significantly improves rooting success for multiplication and conservation.

topic: Distinguishing from Similar Species (F. indica & F. inermis)
question_prompt: How do you distinguish Flacourtia montana from Flacourtia indica?
text: Field Distinction from Flacourtia indica: F. montana has pubescent (hairy) young twigs and leaves that turn a characteristic brown color on drying, whereas F. indica has glabrous (smooth) young twigs and leaves that do not turn brown on drying. Additionally, flower size and cherry-sized scarlet ribbed fruits help confirm F. montana. Note that 'Flacourtia inermis Miq. ex Hook. f. & Thomson' appears as an ambiguous historical synonym in some Indian records and should not be conflated with the distinct species Flacourtia inermis Roxb.
